title: Grant proposals rejected by ‘AI triage’ to be reassessed
key_facts: CRANE, a UK network supported by UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) that aims to strengthen UK cybersecurity research, has written to researchers to apologise and promised to review all proposals again, after it used an AI 'triage' to decide which of the 179 proposals in its latest funding call would go to human review.
Almost half of the applications were rejected by the AI and were not looked at by humans.
CRANE's update says it ran the AI triage with care, with human sampling, statistical cross-checking and confidentiality, but was not transparent enough about it, and is sorry.

CRANE says it will re-review all applications first screened out using AI and reconvene the funding panel to make decisions; offers previously issued are suspended and applicants have been contacted directly.
The call was the CRANE phase one pilot, hosted at the University of Oxford and funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council, a UKRI subsidiary.

CRANE says the triage used closed, ring-fenced read-only large language models with no internet access, no public AI service such as ChatGPT, and that proposal data has not been and will not be used for model training.

UKRI had said that releasing confidential material into generative AI tools breaches its confidentiality and integrity policy; UKRI's own recent proposals for handling the growth in applications include in-person interviews for higher-risk awards, more triage by its staff and exploring safe AI-assisted assessment, with a trial comparing AI conclusions on past applications with real decisions.
Both CRANE and UKRI were approached for comment; CRANE's update was seen by Times Higher Education.
quote_evidence: The network, which aims to strengthen the UK’s cybersecurity research, has now written to researchers to apologise, promising to review all the proposals again.

“Although we undertook the AI triage process with care, with human sampling and statistical cross-checking, and in a way that ensured confidentiality, we recognise that we were not transparent enough about this approach, and for that we are sorry,” says the update, seen by Times Higher Education.
Almost half of the applications were rejected by the AI, and were not looked at by humans.
why_it_matters_hint: Researchers whose proposals were screened out by AI get a human review, and CRANE admits it was not transparent enough about using AI; the case concerns one pilot call of 179 proposals.
event_date: Apology and re-review announced by CRANE shortly before 5 Oct 2026; the AI screening and outcry date from late September (THE first reported it on 27 Sep 2026).
notes: Read in full, plus Times Higher Education's first report of 27 Sep 2026 ('AI-only research grant rejection in UKRI-funded call sparks alarm', read in full): AI-based review with several models against seven criteria rejected half of the 179 proposals before any human read them, and academics such as John Stott (Lancaster) and Claire Hardaker (Lancaster) expressed dismay. The pool marks this as a follow-up of Science's 4 Oct 2026 story 'U.K. funder uses AI triage to reject grant proposals—leaving researchers dismayed' (headline only; no edition of ours carried either). Research Professional News headlines of 28 Sep and 5 Oct on the same row were seen but not read. CRANE's statement is quoted by THE from a letter it saw; no second source for the apology.
